tier_reason: First-party benchmark repo (cachegrand/cachegrand-benchmarks, scripts/run-memtier.sh plus raw memtier_stdout.txt files for cachegrand v0.2.1 and Redis v7.0.11) with the CPU model (AMD EPYC 7502P) stated, but no compiler or build flags for the tested binaries and no peer review or independent reproduction; the project's own benchmark code with partial methodology is C, not B.

corrections.claimed_speedup: GET, d128-c25, per load-generation node n01, AGGREGATED AVERAGE of 3 runs: cachegrand v0.2.1 at t16 = 935,576.61 ops/sec (benchmarks/cachegrand/v0.2.1/d128-c25/n01/t16/get/memtier_stdout.txt) vs Redis v7.0.11 at t1 = 71,143.97 ops/sec (benchmarks/redis/v7.0.11/d128-c25/n01/t1/get/memtier_stdout.txt; Redis was only run at t1), approx 13.2x (derived from page data). At matched t1, cachegrand 78,840.39 vs Redis 71,143.97 ops/sec, approx 1.11x (derived from page data). At t64, cachegrand reaches 2,241,838.36 ops/sec on n01, approx 31.5x Redis's t1 figure (derived from page data). The repo README chart sums both load nodes (about 4.5M GET ops/sec for cachegrand at 64 threads vs about 0.14M for Redis at 1 thread). The high-thread ratios also use 16x or 64x more client connections than the Redis run.
corrections.workload: memtier_benchmark (scripts/run-memtier.sh) GET and SET against the Redis-protocol interface, 128-byte values, keys 1,000,000-2,000,000, 120 s per run, 3 runs averaged, from 2 load-generation nodes (n01, n02). tN is the memtier client thread count (-t N, 25 connections per thread per node; the chart calls this '50 clients per thread, 1 Thread per core'). cachegrand v0.2.1 was run at t1-t64 and Redis v7.0.11 only at t1.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 7502P (32c/64t), 8x32GB DDR4-3200, Ubuntu 22.04 (kernel 5.15.0-70), 2x25Gbit Intel XXV710 (bonded). The main server and the load-generation servers use the same spec (per benchmarks/cachegrand/v0.2.1/README.md, which is identical to benchmarks/redis/v7.0.11/README.md).
corrections.caveats: Self-published by the project author and not independently reproduced. Raw memtier outputs and the run script are public, and the CPU is documented, but the compiler and build flags of the benchmarked binaries are not stated. The only compiler mention is an example startup log in the main README showing a v0.3.0 'Release build, compiled using gcc v11.3.0', which is not the benchmarked build. Redis was measured only with 1 memtier thread (25 connections per node), so the large multi-thread ratios compare a multi-threaded server under 16-64x more client connections against single-threaded Redis. At equal load the gain is only about 1.1x. The benchmark data is licensed CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 and run-memtier.sh is GPL-3.0. The main repo's last commit was 2025-01-02, so it is stale.

notes: The original benchmark_url is a single cachegrand-only memtier output; its 935,576.61 figure is correct, and the Redis figure 71,143.97 is correct but comes from the separate redis/v7.0.11 file, so I repointed benchmark_url to the benchmark repo root, whose README chart compares against Redis, KeyDB and Dragonfly. The record said the tN folders were server worker-thread counts, but per scripts/run-memtier.sh they are memtier client thread counts; I corrected this. Metadata checked via gh: BSD-3-Clause, 1,002 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2025-01-02.

tier_reason: Peer-reviewed OSDI 2020 paper (Berg et al.), Section 5.1 and Figure 12, compares CacheLib against Memcached v1.6.6 using CacheBench (which ships in the CacheLib repo) and states 'up to 60% more requests per second than Memcached'. The paper gives no CPU model, compiler or flags for this experiment, so it cannot be A.

corrections.caveats: The benchmark comes from the CacheLib design paper by its own authors (Berg et al., OSDI 2020). CacheBench was extended to drive an in-process version of a minimally changed Memcached v1.6.6, not the networked Memcached server, and both systems used LRU eviction with 32 threads. The comparison uses CacheLib's default T = 60 s, and the paper notes that T = 10 s raises hit ratio at the cost of lower throughput. CacheBench is public in the CacheLib repo, but the evaluation does not state the CPU model or compiler/build flags, so it falls short of tier A. No independent third-party reproduction was found.

notes: The quoted claim, workload (100M objects, 8-144GB caches, 32 threads, LRU on both) and 'minimally changed Memcached v1.6.6' all match the paper text verbatim. Metadata checked via gh: Apache-2.0, 1,595 stars, not a fork, not archived, last commit 2026-09-26. I only expanded the caveats to cover the in-process Memcached target and the T = 60 s setting.
